author: Ka'Tani Gouch
title: Ottawa County is not getting rid of its Native Plant Project, commissioners say - NewsBreak
text:
By Ka'Tani Gouch ,
2 hours ago OLIVE TOWNSHIP, Mich. (WOOD) — Concerns that Ottawa County’s Native Plant Project was being destroyed sparked confusion this week, prompting county commissioners to reassure residents the project remains safe.
The project , which launched in 2023, was created to address growing groundwater concerns in the county. According to the county’s website, the initiative aims to “reduce water consumption, as well as the time and money on landscaping maintenance.”
Why Ottawa County is short on water and what’s being done about it “The native plants require less water so it’s less demand for resources there,” Ottawa County Commissioner Jim Barry explained.
But recent discussions among board members and the interim county administrator about the look and placement of landscaping at the Fillmore Street Complex raised new questions.
Ottawa County’s Fillmore Street Complex. (Oct. 1, 2025) “Some of the landscaping that’s closer to the door we’re gonna have to possibly move some things around cause it’s creating some damage to some sidewalks and just the aesthetics of how it looks at the entrance,” Barry said.
When community members saw maintenance crews clearing greenery on the property earlier this week, many feared the Native Plant Project itself was being ripped out.
“We got some emails on this and there was some chatter on social media about everything… concern about protecting and keeping the native plant project here on campus at Ottawa County Admin Center,” Barry said.
ArtPrize piece called ‘Give!’ highlights local nature restoration According to Barry, however, it was all a misunderstanding.
“They were clearing out some old beach grass that was actually — I was told was planted in the 1990s and was never a part of the Native Plant Project. But it’s right next to the Native Plant Project so I can understand how there could’ve been some concern,” Barry said.
He emphasized that the project remains intact and that no one wants to remove it.
“Nothing in the Native Plant Project is going to be touched at this point,” Barry said. “We want nothing but the best. We love the Native Plant Project, but we need it to work with the building.”
Barry acknowledged that communication with the public could have been clearer.
“My takeaway is we wanna do a better job of communicating with people that have concerns and care about the Native Plant Project,” Barry said. “We love it and we’re glad we’ve got it and we’re going to protect it.”
Several native flowers were mixed in with the old grass that was dug up, but Barry said those seeds were harvested and will be replanted with new grass at the site.
